title: The Day American Battleships Shelled Japan's Homeland
fullText: July 14th, 1945. Northern Honshu, Japan. A coastline. The water off Kamishi is gray and cold, even in the middle of summer. Smoke rises from the iron works in land. The furnaces burning coal as they have burned it every morning for longer than anyone working there can remember. Then on the horizon, shapes, gray holes, massive, deliberate, not hiding. They come in column, flags flying, growing larger with each minute. They could see the ships from shore. The muzzle flash comes before the sound. Even at this distance, it is enormous. A wall of orange light, brief as a camera shutter, then gone. A long pause. Then the sound arrives like something breaking deep in the earth. On the howiards of USS South Dakota, a signal flag runs up. Every ship in the force can read it. Never forget Pearl Harbor. The Pacific War began with Japanese aircraft destroying the American battleship fleet at Pearl Harbor. It ended with American battleships standing off Japan's coast, shelling her cities while the Imperial Japanese Navy chose not to respond. This is how that happened and what both sides knew that the other didn't. December 7th, 1941. Pearl Harbor, 7:57 in the morning. 353 Japanese aircraft fall on the Pacific Fleet in two waves. In two hours, they do what no enemy has done in living memory. They put the American battle line on the bottom of the harbor. Arizona, Oklahoma, West Virginia, California, Nevada. Five battleships sunk or capsized before breakfast. The weight that was supposed to hold Japan at arms length is gone. What Japan did not sink at Pearl Harbor and what the United States built to replace what was lost would define the next four years. The Pacific War moves in one direction west. Each island is a step. Guadal Canal, Terawa, Saipan, Lee. Each one another airfield, another anchorage. The map contracting from Japan's point of view. By early 1945, the United States Navy has built something that has never existed before. Task Force 58, 16 aircraft carriers, eight fast battleships, 20 cruisers, 80 destroyers, more than a thousand combat aircraft, fighters, dive bombers, torpedo bombers launchable in under an hour. The force has been forged battle by battle. From the turkey shoot in the Philippine Sea to the grinding campaigns from Truck to Lon. It is now large enough, fast enough, and powerful enough not to raid Japan from the margins, but to go directly to the capital. In February 1945, it anchors at Ulithi Atol in the Caroline Islands. The men get three beers on the beach at Mog Mog and wait. The destination is classified. The man commanding this force sits at the rear of his bridge facing the stern. He wears a long build baseball cap with the grommet removed so the brim flops forward. A distinctive unmilitary piece of headgear that has become the most recognizable silhouette in the Pacific Fleet. His brown leather aviator's shoes are non-regulation. When he gives orders, he whispers them. His name is Vice Admiral Mark Andrew Mitcher. He is 57 years old and looks a decade past it. His face is leathered and deeply lined. His frame is slight, almost gaunt. At Annapapolis, he was a catastrophe. 159 demerits in a single class year. He resigned in 1906. His father pulled strings and got him reinstated. He graduated in 1910, 113th out of 131 classmates. What he was even then was a flyer. Naval aviator number 33. He went to sea and didn't come back from it. Ship after ship, year after year, the carrier Navy growing up around him. His chief of staff, Commodore Arley Burke, put it simply, his flyers worshiped him. The war correspondent Ernie Pile met him just before the Tokyo raids and wrote afterward, "From now on, Mitch is one of my gods. He looked out for his pilots. He had been a downed flyer himself. He understood what it meant to be in the water, waiting." His rescue operations for downed air crew had become legend in the fleet. In October 1941, he was given command of a new carrier, USS Hornet. On April 18th, 1942, Captain Mark Mitcher stood on Hornets's Bridge and watched Jimmy Doolittle's 16 B-25 bombers roll down the flight deck and lift into the North Pacific sky. The first American aircraft ever to bomb Tokyo. It was a one-way raid. Hornet could carry the planes to within 650 mi of Japan, but could not recover them. The crews knew this when they took off. Mitcher, watch them go. He is coming back now. The man on Hornet's Bridge in 1942 is the man commanding these 16 carriers, this thousand plane armada, sitting backward in his swivel chair, watching the gray North Pacific swells, saying nothing above a whisper. On February 10th, 1945, Task Force 58 slips away from Uly. Of course, northeast, the destination still classified for most aboard. The fleet drives north through North Pacific winter. Swells 10 to 15 ft. Gray green water, gray sky, gray holes. The temperature drops steadily. At altitude, it will be cold enough to freeze the gun mechanisms in the wing wells of the fighters. On the evening of February 15th, the fleet changes course to the northwest and accelerates. The mission is announced over the ship's intercoms. In 2 days, these carriers will launch the first American strikes against Tokyo since dittle in 1942. No one sleeps. More than half the air groups in Task Force 58 have never flown a combat mission. The men who have are thinking about what they know. The men who haven't are thinking about what they don't. In the bunks and passageways of 16 carriers 60 mi off the coast of Japan, a few thousand pilots and air crew spend the night with their own company. Dawn, February 16th, 1945. The flight decks are full. Hellcats and hell divers and Avengers spotted and armed. Engines turning up, exhaust vapors tearing away in the cold wind. The nearest carrier, Hornet, flagship of Task Group 58.1, is 80 mi from the Japanese coastline. The launch begins. The mission is not to flatten Tokyo. The Marines go ashore on Ewima in 3 days. That small volcanic island hosts Japanese airfields capable of throwing air strikes against the invasion fleet throughout the landing. The airfields around Tokyo are the real target. Disrupt them. Destroy what can be destroyed. Deny Japan the ability to mass its air power against the beaches. That is what this fleet has come to do. For two solid days, American aircraft are over the Tokyo area and Tokyo Bay. Task group 58.5 Enterprise and Saratoga. The fleet's night trained carrier division maintains coverage through the dark hours. night hellcats hunting over Japanese fields and keeping them from recovering. Japan had absorbed months of B-29 strikes from the Maranas. She has never seen this. Enemy carrier fighters over the capital. Ships on the water 60 mi from shore. The B29 was a sound from high altitude, a flash, a distant fire. This is something else entirely. The guns freeze in some of the wing wells. The pilots clear them and keep flying. American aviators claim 341 Japanese aircraft shot down and nearly 200 more destroyed on the ground. Japan's Imperial General Headquarters admits to 78. The truth lies somewhere between. What is not in dispute is what was achieved. The airfields around Tokyo are disrupted. Japan cannot mass its remaining air power against the Eoima beaches. Three days later, when the Marines wait ashore, they face what they face, but not everything. Task Force 58 sails south. In two days of operations, 60 mi off the Japanese coast, not one of its ships is hit. 5 days later, the bill comes. February 21st, Task Force 58 is offima, its carriers flying roundthe-clock support for the Marines ashore. Among them is USS Saratoga CV3, the oldest carrier in the fleet. Laid down as a battle cruiser in 1920 and converted under the Washington Naval Treaty before completion. She has been fighting since the first day of the war. She has come back from damage before. She has come back from everything. The Kamicazis hit her five times. When the fires are out, Saratoga's flight deck is torn and useless. She will be repaired, but she will never return to the Pacific. The ship that survived Guadal Canal in the Solomons and came all the way back to Japan's coast is done. The chain of consequence, though, is already running. The Tokyo carrier raids disrupted Japan's air power in the north. Disrupted air power meant the Marines at Ioima faced a manageable battle rather than sustained air assault throughout. once taken gives the B29 campaign something it has desperately needed. Emergency landing fields for damaged bombers, air strips close enough for fighter escorts. The chain runs from February to August. There is one more link. It will take until August to close. By the summer of 1945, the United States Navy has a problem it could not have imagined in December 1941. The Imperial Japanese Navy is dead in harbor. The great fleet that fought from Pearl Harbor to Laty Gulf. The carriers, the battleships, the cruisers crippled by air attack, paralyzed by fuel starvation. Of the 12 battleships Japan operated during the war, not one is in fighting condition. And so the United States Navy, which went to war because its battleships were sunk, finds itself in the summer of 1945 with a surplus of battleships and nothing for them to fight. The decision to use them against Japan's industrial coastline carries both strategic purpose and something less easily stated in official orders. The Navy's senior leadership wanted to close an account. The ships that survived Pearl Harbor rebuilt, repaired. The ships laid down in the years since to replace what was lost. They were going to Japan. They were going to fire at Japan's cities with 16-in guns from close enough that the people on shore could watch it happen. July 14th, 1945. Northern Honshu, midday, Kamayishi. The signal flag runs up South Dakota's Howiards. Never forget Pearl Harbor. An hour later, the guns open on the Japan Iron and Steel Company's works. The battleships fire from 27 km out, moving steadily closer. The concussion from their shells overturns cooking stoves across the city, starting fires that spread before anyone can reach them. Shore batteries return fire. Their shells fall short and wide. In 2 hours, 8002 rounds fall on the steel plant. What the men on those ships do not know and will not learn until after the war is over is that Allied prisoners of war are being held in camps near the Kamishi iron works. 32 of them are killed in the bombardment. The signal flag said, "Never forget Pearl Harbor." The men flying that signal had no idea they were shelling their own. On the same day, hundreds of miles to the north, a second force hits Moruran on Hawkkaido, Japan's second island beyond the range of the B-29s, a place where the war has until now been distant. Fast battleships Iowa, Missouri, and Wisconsin open fire on the Nihon Steel Company and the Wanishi Iron Works. Iowa finds the furnaces on the second salvo. A massive explosion from Missouri's guns is visible from miles away. Hokkaido had been a distant war until this morning. Three nights later, the largest battleship bombardment of the campaign begins in rain and fog. Hitachi, an industrial city 80 mi northeast of Tokyo. The weather is too poor for spotting aircraft. Six allied battleships, Iowa, Missouri, Wisconsin, North Carolina, Alabama, and HMS King George V of the Royal Navy aim entirely by radar. They open fire at 11 at night. The muzzle flashes illuminate the sea for miles in every direction. The city catches fire. The flames are visible from the ships. By the time the guns stop at 1 in the morning, the American battleships alone have fired 1,238 16in shells. Britain is here. The Royal Navy, which lost Repulse and Prince of Wales to Japanese aircraft in December 1941, stands off Japan's coast in the rain and puts 14in shells into her factories. The next morning, 30,000 people walk out of Hitachi and do not come back. Hitachi had already endured 30 air raids before this night. The people knew bombs. The sound of B-29s at altitude, the flash from high up, the distant thunder of high explosive. They had survived 30 raids. They had never seen this. The B29 was invisible. The battleships were not. No official statement, no government reassurance, explains Gray Hulls sitting on the water off your coast with their guns trained on your city. The war their government had promised them, the inviable homeland, the divine wind driving all invaders back, was visible on the horizon, and it was steel. Japan knew. Imperial General Headquarters had anticipated the naval bombardments. They had planned for them. The decision made in Tokyo was not ignorance or incapacity, but deliberate calculation. Do not respond. Roughly 5,000 aircraft sat on Japanese air strips through these weeks, grounded, fueled, armed, waiting. Kamicazi pilots trained, fighter pilots flew practice sorties. The aircraft were there. The order to use them against the battleships never came. Japan's military planners understood correctly as far as they knew that the Americans would eventually have to invade the home islands. Every aircraft lost in the summer of 1945. Every pilot killed over a coastal bombardment zone was one less weapon for the only battle that now mattered. The decisive beach battle, Ketu go. The entire surviving military capacity of the Japanese Empire, every aircraft, every gun, every suicide boat was being held in absolute reserve for the moment Allied soldiers tried to come ashore. So Japan watched American battleships Shell Kamishi and Moruran and Hitachi held its forces down and waited for the thing it was certain was coming. What Japan could not know, what no one standing on the shore of Honshu could know was that the invasion was already unnecessary. In the desert of New Mexico, a weapon had been built, tested, and was waiting. Two of them, the 5,000 aircraft being preserved for the beaches, would never fly against an invasion. The invasion would never come. The Japanese high command sat with its calculation and held its nerve and waited for a battle that had already been made irrelevant by something they had never been told existed. The grounded planes sat in their rows. The engines stayed cold. August 9th, 1945. Battleships South Dakota, Indiana, and Massachusetts returned to the Kamishi iron works. the same target as July 14th. 8316in shells fall on what is left of the plant. It is the last battleship bombardment of Japan. At this same moment, on the other side of Honshu, the second atomic bomb falls on Nagasaki. The battleship crews do not know. Japan's high command does not know. The people of Kamayishi do not know. On opposite sides of the same island, the last act of the old war and the decisive act of the new one are happening simultaneously, and no one on either shore can see across the mountains. The shells fall in the north. The bomb falls in the south. 6 days later, Japan surrenders. On September 2nd, 1945, USS Missouri drops anchor in Tokyo Bay. The surrender ceremony is held on her fan tail. Representatives of the Japanese government come aboard and sign the instrument of surrender on the deck of a battleship that two months earlier was firing 16-in shells into Japanese steel mills. The same guns, the same ship. The war ends where the shelling stopped. Mark Mitcher had gone home in July before any of this. He was relieved of command and ordered back to Washington. He was 58 years old and looked 70, lean and gray and very quiet. The men who saw him at the end described a man who had given the work everything he had. He died on February 3rd, 1947 at the Naval Hospital in Norfolk, Virginia. Coronary thrombosis. He was 60 years old. His Navy Cross citation for the period January to May 1945 reads in part, "Penetrated enemy home waters to the shores of the main Japanese islands, striking airfields and installations in the Tokyo and Kyushu area. The language of citations is the language of accumulation, dates, areas, objectives. What it does not record is the long road from Annapapolis to Hornet to the backward chair on the flag bridge of a 16 carrier fleet. The whispered orders, the pilots going out and coming back and going out again, the face growing more leathered each month, the bodies spending down what it had. The war did not kill him the way wars kill. But it used him, and what was left when it was done was not enough to last. Admiral Nimmitz said of him, "It is doubtful if any officer has made more important contributions than he toward extinction of the enemy fleet." The chain closes here. The Tokyo carrier raids disrupted the air power that would have bled the Euoima landings. Ewima gave the B29 campaign fighter escorts and emergency landing strips. The B-29 campaign delivered what finished the war. That chain begins with Mitcher sitting backward in his chair on the flag bridge of a carrier 60 mi from Japan, watching the planes go off into the gray North Pacific Dawn. One last ship, the Nagato, Japan's great battleship, the one from whose bridge Admiral Yamamoto ordered the attack on Pearl Harbor, was still afloat when the war ended. She was the only Japanese battleship that was. The others had been sunk at sea or bombed in harbor or left listing in their anchorages. The Nagato survived everything. After the surrender, she was handed over to the United States. In 1946, she was towed to Bikini Atole in the Marshall Islands and used as a target in the Operation Crossroads nuclear tests. She survived the first blast. The second underwater detonation sank her. The age of the battleship ended where the age of the atomic bomb began. The carriers that opened the door to Japan in February 1945 were already the future. The battleships that stood off her coast that summer were already the past. They had their moment. The signal flag running up, the guns turning toward the shore, the shells falling on the steel plants while people on the hillside watched and understood, perhaps before anyone said it plainly, that the war their government had promised them was over. It was enough.
fullTextVi: Ngày 14 tháng 7 năm 1945. Bắc Honshu, Nhật Bản. Một bờ biển. Nước ngoài khơi Kamishi có màu xám và lạnh, ngay cả giữa mùa hè. Khói bốc lên từ các công trình sắt trên đất liền. Những lò đốt than như họ đã đốt nó vào mỗi buổi sáng lâu hơn bất cứ ai làm việc ở đó đều có thể nhớ. Rồi ở phía chân trời, những hình thù, những hố xám, đồ sộ, có chủ ý, không che giấu. Họ đi thành từng hàng, cờ tung bay, lớn dần theo từng phút. Họ có thể nhìn thấy những con tàu từ bờ biển. Đèn flash của mõm xuất hiện trước âm thanh. Ngay cả ở khoảng cách này, nó vẫn rất lớn. Một bức tường ánh sáng màu cam, ngắn gọn như màn trập máy ảnh, rồi biến mất. Một khoảng dừng dài. Sau đó âm thanh vang lên như có thứ gì đó vỡ sâu trong lòng đất. Trên mạn tàu USS South Dakota, một lá cờ hiệu được treo lên. Mọi tàu trong lực lượng đều có thể đọc được nó. Đừng bao giờ quên Trân Châu Cảng. Chiến tranh Thái Bình Dương bắt đầu bằng việc máy bay Nhật tiêu diệt hạm đội thiết giáp hạm Mỹ tại Pearl Cảng. Nó kết thúc với việc các thiết giáp hạm Mỹ đứng ngoài khơi bờ biển Nhật Bản, pháo kích vào các thành phố của Nhật Bản trong khi Hải quân Đế quốc Nhật Bản quyết định không trả lời. Đây là cách điều đó đã xảy ra và điều mà cả hai bên đều biết còn bên kia thì không. Ngày 7 tháng 12 năm 1941. Trân Châu Cảng, 7:57 sáng. 353 máy bay Nhật rơi xuống Hạm đội Thái Bình Dương thành hai đợt. Trong hai giờ, họ làm được điều mà trong ký ức sống chưa từng có kẻ thù nào làm được. Họ đặt chiến tuyến của Mỹ dưới đáy bến cảng. Arizona, Oklahoma, Tây Virginia, California, Nevada. Năm thiết giáp hạm bị đánh chìm hoặc lật úp trước bữa sáng. Sức nặng đáng lẽ phải giữ Nhật Bản trong tầm tay đã không còn nữa. Những gì Nhật Bản không đánh chìm ở Trân Châu Cảng và những gì Hoa Kỳ đã xây dựng để thay thế những gì đã mất sẽ quyết định bốn năm tới. Chiến tranh Thái Bình Dương di chuyển theo một hướng về phía tây. Mỗi hòn đảo là một bước. Kênh Guadal, Terawa, Saipan, Lee. Mỗi sân bay khác, một nơi neo đậu khác. Bản đồ thu hẹp theo quan điểm của Nhật Bản. Đến đầu năm 1945, Hải quân Hoa Kỳ đã chế tạo được thứ chưa từng tồn tại trước. Lực lượng Đặc nhiệm 58, 16 tàu sân bay, 8 thiết giáp hạm nhanh, 20 tàu tuần dương, 80 tàu khu trục, hơn thế nữa hơn một nghìn máy bay chiến đấu, máy bay chiến đấu, máy bay ném bom bổ nhào, máy bay ném ngư lôi có thể phóng trong hour. Lực lượng đã được tôi luyện qua từng trận chiến. Từ cuộc bắn gà tây ở Biển Philippine đến các chiến dịch nghiền nát của Xe tải tới Lon. Bây giờ nó đủ lớn, đủ nhanh và đủ mạnh để không tấn công Nhật Bản từ bên lề mà đi thẳng tới thủ đô. Vào tháng 2 năm 1945, nó neo đậu tại Ulithi Atol thuộc Quần đảo Caroline. Những người đàn ông lấy ba cốc bia trên bãi biển ở Mog Mog và chờ đợi. Điểm đến đã được phân loại. Người chỉ huy lực lượng này ngồi ở phía sau cầu đối diện với nghiêm khắc. Anh ấy đội một chiếc mũ bóng chày dài đã được tháo bỏ vòng đệm để vành lộn nhào về phía trước. Một chiếc mũ đội đầu phi quân sự đặc biệt đã trở thành hình bóng dễ nhận biết nhất trong Hạm đội Thái Bình Dương. Đôi giày phi công bằng da màu nâu của anh ấy không theo quy định. Khi ra lệnh, anh ấy thì thầm chúng. Tên ông ấy là Phó Đô đốc Mark Andrew Mitcher. Ông ấy đã 57 tuổi và trông như đã qua cả chục năm rồi. Khuôn mặt của anh ta được bọc da và có đường nhăn sâu. Thân hình ông gầy gò, gần như gầy gò. Ở Annapapolis, anh ấy là một thảm họa. 159 điểm kém trong một năm học. Ông từ chức năm 1906. Cha anh đã giật dây và bắt anh phục hồi chức vụ. Ông tốt nghiệp năm 1910, đứng thứ 113 trong số 131 bạn cùng lớp. Lúc đó anh ấy thậm chí còn là một người bay. Phi công hải quân số 33. Anh ta đã đi biển và không trở về. Hết con tàu này đến con tàu khác, năm này qua năm khác, hàng không mẫu hạm Hải quân ngày càng lớn lên xung quanh ông. Tham mưu trưởng của ông, Commodore Arley Burke, nói một cách đơn giản, những người truyền thông tôn thờ ông. Phóng viên chiến trường Ernie Pile đã gặp anh ta ngay trước cuộc đột kích ở Tokyo và viết sau đó, "Từ giờ trở đi, Mitch là một trong những vị thần của tôi. Anh ấy trông chừng các phi công của mình. Bản thân anh ấy cũng là một người rơi máy bay. Anh ấy hiểu ý nghĩa của việc ở dưới nước, chờ đợi. " Hoạt động giải cứu phi hành đoàn bị bắn rơi của anh ấy đã trở thành huyền thoại trong hạm đội. Vào tháng 10 năm 1941, ông được giao quyền chỉ huy tàu sân bay mới USS Hornet. Vào ngày 18 tháng 4 năm 1942, Thuyền trưởng Mark Mitcher đứng trên Cầu Hornets và quan sát Jimmy 16 máy bay ném bom B-25 của Doolittle lăn xuống sàn đáp và bay lên phía Bắc Bầu trời Thái Bình Dương. Máy bay Mỹ đầu tiên ném bom Tokyo. Đó là một cuộc đột kích một chiều. Hornet có thể mang máy bay đến phạm vi 650 dặm cách Nhật Bản, nhưng không thể phục hồi chúng. Các phi hành đoàn biết điều này khi họ cất cánh. Mitcher, coi chừng họ đi. Bây giờ anh ấy đang quay lại. Người đàn ông trên cầu Hornet năm 1942 là người chỉ huy 16 tàu sân bay này, Chiếc hạm đội ngàn máy bay này, ngồi ngả lưng trên chiếc ghế xoay, nhìn về phương Bắc xám xịt Thái Bình Dương dâng trào, không nói gì hơn là thì thầm. Ngày 10/2/1945, Chiến đoàn 58 rút lui khỏi Uly. Tất nhiên, hướng đông bắc, điểm đến vẫn được phân loại dành cho hầu hết người trên tàu. Hạm đội lái xe về phía bắc qua mùa đông Bắc Thái Bình Dương. Sưng lên từ 10 đến 15 ft. Nước xanh xám, bầu trời xám, hố xám. Nhiệt độ giảm dần. Ở độ cao, trời sẽ đủ lạnh để đóng băng cơ chế súng trong giếng cánh của máy bay chiến đấu. Tối 15/2, hạm đội chuyển hướng về hướng Tây Bắc và tăng tốc. Nhiệm vụ được thông báo qua hệ thống liên lạc nội bộ của tàu. Trong 2 ngày nữa, các tàu sân bay này sẽ tiến hành cuộc tấn công đầu tiên của Mỹ vào Tokyo kể từ nhỏ vào năm 1942. Không ai ngủ. Hơn một nửa phi đội trong Lực lượng Đặc nhiệm 58 chưa bao giờ bay nhiệm vụ chiến đấu. Những người đàn ông đang suy nghĩ về những gì họ biết.
